hook: A bathtub fills from the tap while the drain is open. Whether the water rises or falls at any moment depends on one comparison: is more coming in than going out? How much water is in the tub at 7:10 depends on how much was there at 7:00, plus everything that came in, minus everything that drained, in between. That bookkeeping is one integral.

prereq.why: The integral of a rate of change is the net change.

prereq.q: A trapezoidal sum on a subinterval of width 3 with endpoint values 4 and 10 adds

figure.caption: Water flows in at R(t) and out at D(t). The amount rises while R > D, falls while D > R, and peaks where the rates cross at t = 6.

chain.cause: A quantity gains at a rate in and loses at a rate out
chain.effect: its net rate of change is $A'(t) = R(t) - D(t)$

chain.cause: Integrate the net rate over an interval
chain.effect: the net change in the amount: $\int_a^b (R(t) - D(t))\,dt$

chain.cause: Add the amount at the start

chain.effect: the amount has a relative extremum there; compare it with the endpoints to find the absolute one

ideas: Amount now = amount at the start + $\int$ (rate in − rate out). The initial amount is part of the answer.
$A'(t) = R(t) - D(t)$: the amount increases when the rate in is larger and decreases when the rate out is larger.
An integral of a rate has the accumulated unit: gallons per hour integrated over hours gives gallons.
An interpretation names the quantity, its units and the time interval.
For the greatest or least amount on a closed interval: find where R − D changes sign, then compare with the endpoints (candidates test).

misconception.wrong: The tank holds 50 L at $t = 0$, so at $t = 9$ it holds $\int_0^9 (R(t) - D(t))\,dt$ liters.
misconception.right: That integral is the change in the amount. The amount itself is $50 + \int_0^9 (R(t) - D(t))\,dt$.

summary: With a rate in $R$ and a rate out $D$, the amount satisfies $A'(t) = R(t) - D(t)$ and $A(t) = A(a) + \int_a^t (R - D)$. Integrals of rates carry accumulated units and need an interpretation with quantity, units and interval. The amount peaks or bottoms out where $R - D$ changes sign or at an endpoint.
